Divine speech to Moses opens the camp-pu: Three excluded groups are retained: leprous, with seminal discharge, and unclean through a dead person. The last phrase is contextual corpse impurity, not a claim that souls themselves contaminate.
Male and female are both included; the emphatic prohibition and God's dwelling among them remain. Plural camps follows the selected Greek.
Israel's action and the repeated correspondence to the Lord's command are both represented.
A new speech marks the shift from camp impurity to restitution.
Both man and woman can incur guilt. Utter disregard represents the emphatic repeated verb without supplying an unexpressed object such as the Lord.
Confession precedes repayment of principal plus one fifth to the wronged person. Neither the amount nor the recipient changes.
Absent next of kin, restitution belongs to the priest as payment to the Lord. The ram of atonement is additional, not included in the repayment.
The first portion of consecrated things brought to the Lord and priest belongs to the priest. Both recipient expressions are retained.
The repeated possessive his remains in the two clauses, preserving the compact ownership wording.
column3: The referent of his in the first clause requires fuller syntactic review; the draft does not resolve it by an added name.

Divine speech to Moses opens the camp-pu: The divine speech formula introduces the jealousy procedure.
Any man's wife and her emphatic disregard of him remain the conditional starting point.
Sexual intercourse, concealment, absence of a witness and not being caught are distinct conditions. The English does not convert suspicion into proof.
The two jealousy cases explicitly include both actual defilement and its absence. Both alternatives remain fully stated.
The husband brings wife and barley gift; one tenth of an oiphi, no oil and no frankincense are preserved. The memorial brings sin to remembrance.
The priest brings and positions the woman before the Lord; she is the object of both actions.
Clean and living both qualify the water. Earth comes from the tent floor and is placed into the earthenware vessel's water.
Uncovering the head is retained without interpreting a hairstyle. The offering rests on her hands while the testing water remains in the priest's hand.
column3: The terminology of testing/reproof needs a fuller lexical comparison; no replacement is asserted here.

Divine speech to Moses opens the camp-pu: The oath's innocent condition has two negatives. Be unharmed expresses immunity from the curse water, without declaring the procedure already completed.
The Greek's or between transgression and defilement remains. The other partner is explicitly someone besides her husband.
The priest pronounces the curse; the Lord is the named agent of its effect. Thigh collapse and belly swelling are preserved without specifying an unexpressed medical mechanism.
The water enters the belly and the bodily clauses repeat. The woman's doubled assent remains doubled.
The curses are written on a scroll and wiped into the water. The draft does not add ink or a recipe absent from the wording.
The priest makes her drink and the water enters her. This anticipatory statement remains beside the later drinking instruction rather than being deleted as repetition.
The priest takes the offering from her hand, places it before the Lord and brings it toward the altar. No waving motion is supplied.
A handful constitutes the memorial portion; altar offering precedes the drinking instruction in this sentence.
Defilement with concealment remains the condition of the stated curse effects. The text's bodily expressions and public curse remain unexpanded.
Not defiled and clean are both stated, followed by immunity and bringing forth seed. No pregnancy is assumed at the start of the procedure.
The summary identifies the law of jealousy and the married woman's transgression and defilement.
The alternative jealousy case names the husband and then the priest's performance of the entire law. It is not limited to the guilty case.
The man is free from sin while the woman bears her sin. The asymmetry is retained rather than editorially softened.
Divine speech opens the vow legislation.
A man or woman may solemnly make the vow. The sentence continues into separation from wine in verse 3; no missing designation is supplied from another text.
Wine, strong drink, both vinegars, grape preparations, fresh grapes and raisins are all retained. Repeated separation from wine is not dropped.
The comprehensive vine restriction includes the selected Greek's wine and the endpoints pressed skins and seed.
column3: The compressed coordination of wine with the skins-to-seed phrase remains awkward and needs fuller syntax and lexical review.

Divine speech to Moses opens the camp-pu: No razor touches the head throughout the vow; holiness and growing hair last until the vowed days are fulfilled.
The prohibition concerns entering where any dead person is during the vow, without reducing it to touching a corpse.
Father, mother, brother and sister are individually named. The vow upon the head explains the restriction even when these relatives die.
Holiness unto the Lord covers all the vow's days, retaining the repeated all.
Sudden nearby death immediately defiles the vowed head. Cleansing-day shaving and seventh-day shaving both remain.
Two turtledoves or two young pigeons are brought on the eighth day to the priest at the tent doors.
The priest prepares separate sin and whole burnt offerings, makes atonement concerning the dead person and consecrates the head that day.
The selected relative clause whereon he was consecrated remains linked to verse 11. A year-old guilt lamb and cancellation of former days follow.
column3: The unusual relative-clause syntax requires apparatus and syntactic review; no conventional reconsecration formula is substituted.

Divine speech to Moses opens the camp-pu: The vow's fulfilment brings presentation at the tent doors. His offering is an English completion of the presenting verb from the following gift list, not an additional object.
Male lamb, ewe lamb and ram are distinguished, all unblemished; year-old modifies the first two. Their three offering functions remain separate.
The basket contains oil-prepared loaves and oil-spread wafers. Associated sacrifice and drink offering are retained.
The priest presents the offerings and prepares the sin and whole burnt offerings in the stated order.
The ram is the deliverance sacrifice, with the unleavened basket and accompanying sacrifice and drink offering.
The vowed person shaves at the tent doors and puts the hair on the fire beneath the deliverance sacrifice. The location and destination are explicit.
The boiled foreleg, one loaf and one wafer are placed in the vowed person's hands after shaving. Hair explicates the vow's metonymic object.
Presentation, priestly holiness, breast and set-apart foreleg remain distinct. Wine becomes permitted afterward; it is not required earlier in the rite.
The vowed gift and whatever the hand can find are distinguished; the extent of the vow remains tied to the consecration law.
column3: The compact relation of means, extent and vow needs a further spoken-language pass before acceptance.

Divine speech to Moses opens the camp-pu: The speech formula introduces the priestly blessing.
Aaron and his sons receive the instruction. The selected Greek places the name-and-blessing clause parenthetically here, before the blessing, and the draft preserves that placement.
Blessing and keeping address the human recipient with you. No divine-address Thou is introduced into this blessing.
The shining face and mercy petitions remain distinct; mercy is retained rather than replaced by a familiar alternative from another tradition.
Lifting the face and granting peace conclude the three petitions. The selected chapter ends here; no separately numbered verse 27 is invented.
